mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement OM651 engine for a C250 CDI typically costs between £800 and £5,200 depending on condition. Used units start from £800-£1,900, reconditioned from £2,500-£4,400, and fully rebuilt from £2,800-£5,200. A replacement OM651.912 engine costs on average £3,850 in good condition, with reconditioned units costing up to £4,409. Labour for supply & fit adds £500-£1,000.

mainEntity.name: Does the C-Class 250 CDI have a timing belt or timing chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: The C250 CDI uses the OM651 engine, which has a single timing chain at the rear of the engine. Unlike the front-mounted duplex chains on earlier OM646 engines, the OM651's rear-mounted chain is prone to stretching. A metallic rattling noise on cold start is the classic warning sign. Some owners have reported chain failure at 90,000 miles, with failure typically occurring between 80,000-120,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in a Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: On OM651-equipped C250 CDI models, the most common symptom is a rattling or clattering noise from the rear of the engine on cold start. Other signs include loss of power, rough idle, engine misfires, and the engine management light illuminating. If you hear any unusual sounds, have the timing system inspected immediately - ignoring the rattle can lead to catastrophic engine failure.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the car's condition and mileage. A W204 C250 CDI is typically worth £4,000-£10,000 - a rebuilt OM651 engine (£2,800-£5,200) can be a worthwhile investment if the car is in good condition. The C250 CDI's strong performance and desirable specification often justify engine replacement. For lower-value examples or those with multiple issues, a specialist repair may be more economical than a full replacement.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the C250 CDI and C220 CDI engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both the C250 CDI and C220 CDI use the OM651 2.1-litre diesel engine, but with significant differences in specification. The C250 CDI produces 204 hp and 500 Nm of torque, compared to the C220 CDI's 170 hp and 400 Nm. The C250 CDI achieves this through a two-stage turbocharging system with a larger main turbo and higher-flow injectors, combined with a smaller turbo for quick low-end response. The result is a 0-62 mph time of 7.0 seconds for the C250 CDI versus 8.4 seconds for the C220 CDI.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI to lose power?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power loss in the C250 CDI is most commonly caused by turbocharger issues, particularly sticking variable vanes on the two-stage turbo system. Other causes include EGR valve clogging, injector seal failure ('Black Death'), and timing chain stretch causing cam timing drift. The two-stage turbo system adds complexity - if the small turbo fails to spool or the large turbo loses boost, power drops significantly. A diagnostic check with Mercedes STAR or compatible equipment is essential to identify the exact cause.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The C250 CDI badge arrived with the W204 generation in 2008 as the range-topping four-cylinder diesel, positioned above the C220 CDI. Powered by the OM651 2.1-litre four-cylinder diesel, it produced 204 hp and a remarkable 500 Nm of torque - figures that rivalled V6 diesels of the era. The C250 CDI utilised a two-stage turbocharging system that combined a small, quick-spooling turbo for low-end response with a larger main turbo for sustained high-end power. The badge continued through the W204 facelift and into the C204 coupe and S204 estate, with BlueEFFICIENCY variants offering improved fuel economy, before being replaced by the C250d in the W205 generation.

milestones.description: OM651.911, 2.1L diesel, 204 hp (150 kW) - W204 C250 CDI launch; two-stage turbocharging; 500 Nm torque; 0-62 mph in 7.0 seconds
Estate (S204) and 4MATIC variants added; OM651.911 engine continues
BlueEFFICIENCY badging introduced; OM651.911 with revised ECU calibration
C204 Coupe launched; C250 CDI variant available; 4MATIC available on saloon
OM651.912 introduced for 4MATIC and certain BlueEFFICIENCY variants
W204 production ends; C250 CDI badge replaced by C250d in W205 generation

problems.h4: OM651 Timing Chain Failure - Why the C250 CDI Rattles on Cold Start
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI (OM651.911, OM651.912 and OM651.916, W204, 2008-2014)
problems.rootCause: The OM651 uses a single timing chain mounted at the rear of the engine, adjacent to the gearbox. The chain stretches over time due to inadequate tensioner design and extended oil change intervals. A metallic rattling or clattering noise on cold start is the classic warning sign. If the chain jumps or snaps, the engine requires cylinder head removal and valve replacement. The OM651 is the same engine used in Mercedes Sprinter vans, with some examples reaching 540,000 miles, but the timing chain remains the critical weak point.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace hydraulic timing chain tensioner only
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught very early; some owners report success with tensioner-only replacement

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of timing chain, tensioners, guides, and sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: Best done at first rattle; prevents catastrophic failure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Cylinder head removal, valve replacement, piston inspection, full timing components
repairOptions.longevity: Required if chain has jumped; bent valves almost certain

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete replacement with professionally rebuilt OM651 unit with upgraded timing components
repairOptions.longevity: Best long-term value on higher-mileage cars

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W204 C250 CDI is worth £4,000-£10,000 depending on condition and mileage. For vehicles under £5,000, a preventative chain replacement (£900-£1,400) is usually the better financial decision than a full engine replacement. For higher-value examples, a rebuilt OM651 with warranty (£2,800-£5,200) offers peace of mind. The C250 CDI's strong performance credentials mean replacement is usually justified for well-maintained cars.
problems.recommendation: If you hear a rattling noise from the rear of the engine on cold starts - especially between 80,000 and 120,000 miles - act immediately. A preventative chain replacement at a specialist (£900-£1,400) saves thousands compared to waiting for failure. Some owners have reported success with replacing just the tensioner, but a full chain and tensioner replacement is the safer long-term solution. Once the chain jumps, piston-to-valve contact is almost certain and engine replacement becomes the only viable option.

problems.h4: OM651 Injector Seal Failure - "Black Death" Carbon Buildup
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI (OM651.911, OM651.912 and OM651.916, W204, 2008-2014)
problems.rootCause: The copper washer seal between the injector and cylinder head degrades over time, allowing combustion gases to escape past the seal. The escaping gas mixes with carbon and unburnt fuel, creating hard, black, crusty deposits around the injector. Early Delphi injectors are particularly prone to failure. Symptoms include a chuffing or ticking noise, a strong diesel smell in the cabin, hissing sounds from the engine, and visible black tar-like residue.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove one injector, clean seat, replace copper washer and clamp bolt
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early; prevents injector seizure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: All four injector seals replaced, carbon removal from bores, leak-off testing
repairOptions.longevity: For moderate carbon buildup; specialist approach significantly cheaper

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Seized injector drilling/extraction, cylinder head removal, injector bore machining
repairOptions.longevity: Required if injector cannot be extracted non-destructively

problems.recommendation: The "Black Death" is insidious but slow-moving. If you hear a ticking or chuffing noise that changes with engine speed, or smell diesel fumes in the cabin, inspect the injector area immediately. Caught early, an £180-£300 single seal replacement is cheap peace of mind. Early Delphi injectors are more prone to failure, so consider replacing all injectors if one has failed.
problems.cta: -> Get quotes for OM651 injector seal replacement for your C250 CDI

problems.h4: OM651 EGR Valve & Turbocharger Issues - Reduced Power and Hesitation
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 250 CDI (OM651.911, OM651.912 and OM651.916, W204, 2008-2014)
problems.rootCause: The EGR valve can become clogged with carbon deposits, particularly on vehicles used for short journeys. The two-stage turbocharger system - with a small turbo for low-end response and a larger main turbo for high-end power - can suffer from sticking variable vanes due to carbon buildup, causing loss of boost and reduced power. EGR clogging is a known issue.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove and clean EGR valve; or replace if necessary
repairOptions.longevity: Viable; carbon buildup is the main cause

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace or rebuild turbocharger, oil feed lines
repairOptions.longevity: Required if turbo has failed or vanes are seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new turbo and EGR components
repairOptions.longevity: Only if turbo failure has caused engine damage

problems.recommendation: If your C250 CDI experiences loss of power, particularly when climbing hills, have the turbocharger and EGR system inspected. A £300-£600 EGR clean or £1,000-£1,800 turbo repair is significantly cheaper than a full engine replacement. Regular motorway driving helps keep the EGR and turbo vanes clear.
